title: Old Mossback
part: PART ONE: SIXTY-ONE CHIMNEYS AND ONE TROLL

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: The troll under the old bridge is enormous, hungry and wicked. Do not look at him. Do not speak to him. Above all, do not ask him questions.*

The town of Bridgewater had four bridges, sixty-one chimneys and one troll, and it was the troll that everybody talked about.

Nobody had actually seen him. That was the trouble. A troll you have never seen can be as large and as terrible as you like, and every year in Bridgewater he grew a little larger and a little more terrible, the way a fish does when it is being described. By the time this story starts, the troll under the old bridge was said to be the size of a haystack, with teeth like garden spades and a temper like a kettle on the boil, and he was known to the whole town, with great affection and no evidence, as Old Mossback.

"Steer clear of Mossback," mothers said, tucking scarves into coats.

"Never mind the weather, mind the bridge," said the old men outside the barber's, and nodded at one another as though they had said something wise.
pages.image: A cozy stone market-town at morning with four humped bridges over a river and many chimneys smoking; the oldest bridge in the middle is mossy and humpbacked, and townspeople crossing the other bridges glance nervously toward it.

pages.text:
Rue Alder, who was ten, knew every rule about the troll by heart. She knew them the way she knew the times tables and the words to the town song, because she was a girl who liked to get things right.

She was small and sturdy and freckled, with curly red-brown hair tied up in two puffs with green yarn, and on this particular morning she was wearing her mustard-yellow raincoat, which had been patched twice, and a pair of rubber boots that had belonged to somebody else's older brother. She was carrying a tray of scones from the Kettle & Crumb, where she lived with her Gran, across three bridges to the doctor's house on the far side of the river.

She did not take the fourth bridge. Nobody did. It was the oldest and the shortest way, and it was humped in the middle like a cat that has heard a noise, and the moss on it was very green, and everyone walked the long way round.

Rue walked the long way round, too. She was good at it.
pages.image: Rue, a small sturdy freckled girl with curly red-brown hair in two puffs tied with green yarn, a patched mustard-yellow raincoat and big rubber boots, carries a tray of scones over a stone bridge, with the mossy humpbacked old bridge visible in the distance behind her.

pages.text:
The Bridgewater schoolhouse had one yard, one chestnut tree and, at half past twelve every day, one very clear arrangement of children. The Bridge Club sat in the middle of the yard, where the sun was. Their leader was Skye Tanner, who was eleven and very tall, with a long fair braid, and who was used to being followed. Next to her, saying most of the words, sat Cedric Pettibone, the Mayor's nephew, who was skinny and slick-haired and wore a red waistcoat as though somebody might be about to take his picture.

The Bridge Club had a game. The game was daring each other to touch the middle stone of the old bridge, and so far nobody had done it, though everybody had said they would.

Rue sat at the very end of the long bench by the wall with her lunch in her lap, and wore a cheerful face, and ate her bread one careful bite at a time. It was a good face. She had been practicing it since spring.

Nobody asked her to join them. She told herself she would not have wanted to.
pages.image: A sunny schoolyard at lunch: on the left, Skye, a tall girl with a long fair braid, and Cedric, a skinny boy in a red waistcoat, laugh with a group of children; on a wooden bench far to the right sits one single lonely girl in a mustard raincoat with curly red-brown hair puffs, eating her lunch alone

pages.text:
Rue had a private rule, and she had made it all by herself: you cannot be lonely if you are useful.

So she was extremely useful. She swept the tea shop floor before she was asked to, and she balanced Gran's accounts in the evenings, and she ran errands for half the street and wrote a long cheerful letter every Sunday to her mother, who captained a river barge called the *Persistent* somewhere far downstream and was, according to the last letter, "still stuck behind a very rude sandbank." Rue fed Biscuit, the shop cat, who was enormous, orange and grateful for nothing. She learned the names of every customer and the way each of them took their tea.

It was surprising how much a person could get done if she never sat still for long enough to notice she was on her own. Rue had done a very great deal, by the end of the summer.

She was tired in a way that sleeping did not fix.
pages.image: Rue in the warm cluttered tea shop sweeping the floor, an enormous orange cat watching her from a stool, a stack of accounting books and a half-written letter on the counter, a pot steaming on the stove behind her.

pages.text:
On the last day of the week, Cedric Pettibone climbed on a crate in the yard and announced that Old Mossback had eaten the baker's sheep.

"Last winter," he said. "All twelve. The wool was still on the bridge."

A gasp went round, the good, satisfied gasp of a crowd being frightened on purpose. It was then that the new boy under the chestnut tree, Perrin Fen, who was thin and quiet and wore a wool hat two sizes too big for him, and who had eaten lunch alone since April, said clearly and to nobody in particular that sheep did not usually go over bridges in the first place, and that there was only one baker, and he had never had twelve.

The yard laughed at him. It was not a cruel laugh, which somehow made it worse.

Rue heard every word. She opened her mouth to say something. She felt her cheerful face slide a little, like a hat in a wind, and she closed her mouth again, and looked at her bread.

It bothered her all afternoon.
pages.image: A skinny boy in a red waistcoat stands on a crate declaring something to a laughing crowd of children in a schoolyard while, under a chestnut tree at the edge, a thin quiet boy in an oversized wool hat looks at the ground, and Rue on her bench looks up with a troubled expression.
